title: Spain’s Solar Eclipses, Russia-Ukraine Drone Warfare, ICE Detention Camp Overcrowding, and Tracking the Spread of Fake News
content: As large swaths of Europe and parts of North America and Africa prepared for a solar eclipse this week, news outlets sought to capture the rare astronomical event that many people may never see again in their lifetime. El Orden Mundial’s visual story explored why Spain is one of the exceptions, with the country set to experience two more eclipses within two years. Our roundup of the Top 10 in Data journalism, looking at stories from July 23 to August 11, also includes a Reuters graphical illustration showing how drones are transforming fighting on the frontlines in Ukraine, an ARIJ investigation examining civilian-to-combatant casualty ratios in the Middle East under different US presidents, and a Straits Times analysis modeling how early debunking can stop the spread of misinformation.

title: Investigating Inside Conflict Zones and Areas Controlled by Armed Groups: Lessons from South Asia and the Middle East
content:
In October 2021, journalist Shahid Zehri was driving home to Karachi through the town of Hub, in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, when a bomb planted under his car seat detonated. He died of his injuries hours later.

The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), a separatist rebel group regarded as a terrorist organization by the Pakistani government and several other countries, including the United States, claimed responsibility, accusing Zehri of spying for Pakistan’s security forces, without offering evidence. “It is intolerable that separatist rebels are able, with impunity, to claim the right to kill journalists in a completely arbitrary manner,” Reporters Without Borders (RSF) spokesperson Pauline Adès-Mével said in a statement in response to the killing.

title: Silencing Journalists Online: How Copyright Is Being Weaponized Against Investigative Journalists
content:
A new form of censorship is emerging globally to silence the work of journalists and activists. On digital platforms like Facebook or Google, journalists’ social media accounts and their stories are being targeted with fake complaints aimed at silencing their work online.

The perpetrators are often shady firms hired by powerful interests who offer to remove content their clients don’t like online by playing with digital platforms rules.

Reputation cleaning firms or individuals make up false claims of copyright infringement and pressure the digital platforms to take down targeted contents. Do they succeed? Often, they do.  And Big Tech companies sometimes even refuse to disclose information on who makes these complaints.

The mechanics are straightforward and hard to fight: scammers duplicate the journalists’ social media accounts or content and file fake copyright infringement claims to digital platforms, accusing the journalists of impersonating them thus violating the platforms’ rules. This results in the journalists’ accounts or posts being suspended or banned, with the victims sometimes not being aware of the reasons they’re kicked out.

title: Strategies To Seek Funding For Investigative Journalism
content:
We are in a challenging environment for investigative journalism. The need for investigative reporting exceeds reliable funding sources for it in many parts of the world. Nonetheless, investigative journalists are approaching the challenges with creativity and resilience, and have multiple paths to explore to seek funding. This session will provide a kind of decision tree or logic to help journalists determine what paths may be worth exploring to find story and project funding in their region or topic. Our talk is aimed at individual journalists who have not done fundraising for their work and are seeking advice on where to get started. We’ll explore key considerations and pathways you can choose depending on your circumstances to explore funding options and pursue those that may fit for you and support the journalism you seek to produce.

This session will not provide suggestions or lists of specific funding sources.  Funding options vary greatly by country, region and even your own individual situations. However, a tip sheet will provide links to global organizations that can help you research grant options, examples of journalism networks and networked funders and some other tips.

title: GIJN Masterclass Round-Up: Data Journalism
content:
GIJN’s Global Academy is your gateway to investigative journalism training. Through masterclass videos, training programs (in person or online), webinars or mentorship programs, the Academy helps journalists at every stage strengthen their investigative skills, connect with peers, and continue learning. In this post, we’ve gathered some of our recent expert masterclass videos that tackle different aspects of using data in your investigations.

In this masterclass video, Fabiola Torres, founder and director of Salud con Lupa, shares a practical approach to data journalism, starting not with tools, but with documents.

She explains how investigations often begin with access to information requests, and how journalists must build their own datasets from messy, fragmented sources like PDFs. Using simple tools like spreadsheets and keyword searches, she shows how to organize, analyze, and extract insights from large volumes of information.

This grounded, hands-on guide cuts through the hype to help: master the basics, trust your reporting instincts, and turn raw data into impactful investigations.

  • Interview: Sarah Ulrich
  • Video Editing: Quentin Egloff
  • Music: Lionel Marçal

title: Can We Gamify That? The Innovators Turning Investigations on Spying Scandals and Vote Rigging into Video Games
content:
An animated phone vibrates on a blackened screen as ominous piano music tinkles in the background. When you click, speech bubbles appear. “It’s Thanasis Koukakis,” the person on the other end says. “I’m borrowing a phone… Just don’t try to reach out to me for now. Texts, calls, try to avoid it.”

This is the opening scene of “Predatorgate,” a new video game based on an investigation into the Predator spyware scandal in Greece. Koukakis was the reporter at the heart of that real-life story who discovered his phone had been infected with the highly invasive spyware. This narrative game is based on the investigation by Inside Story, and shows what it’s like to be in the shoes of a journalist under threat of illegal surveillance. In the game — which takes an estimated 30 minutes to play — Koukakis is a colleague who discovers his phone has been targeted.

title: Open Source Intelligence Researcher
content:
Rappler are seeking an experienced Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) Researcher to join their digital forensics team. This role plays a critical part in executing digital forensics and investigative research to uncover disinformation trends and provide actionable intelligence. You will work closely with editorial units, revenue teams, and brand partners to gather, analyze, and visualize complex datasets that support investigative journalism and revenue-generating data consultancy services.

You are a data-driven investigator with a passion for uncovering the truth within complex information ecosystems. You have a sharp eye for digital footprints and the analytical rigor to incorporate technical and business requirements into deep-dive research.

As a methodical researcher, you know exactly when and why to use specific OSINT tools, always approaching a problem with a clear research goal as your driving factor. You are as comfortable diving into raw datasets and coordinating with institutional sources as you are translating findings for non-technical stakeholders.

title: Bilingual Editor
content:
The Palestine Reporting Lab is seeking an experienced bilingual (Arabic and English) editor to help shape ambitious investigative, research-based, enterprise and narrative journalism about Palestine and Palestinian communities.

The Palestine Reporting Lab supports investigative and in-depth stories that uncover hidden harm, focus on accountability, and serve communities affected by abuses of power. We provide emerging and veteran journalists with rigorous editorial guidance and mentorship, meaningful financial support, and opportunities for collaborative reporting, research, and storytelling.

The Palestine Reporting Lab is not an outlet. Instead, we are a journalism incubator. We develop reporting projects, support reporters and reporting teams to carry them out, and produce and publish our projects in partnership with leading news organizations in English and in Arabic.

The Palestine Reporting Lab is a project of Just Vision, an independent, not-for-profit media organization based in the United States, and is guided by the Society of Professional Journalists’ Code of Ethics. We are committed to editorial independence, truth, integrity, and fairness.

title: Do You Have ‘the OSINT Mindset’?: Try Our Quiz for Those Who Like ‘a Little Light Online Sleuthing’
content:
OSINT, visual investigations, digital sleuthing: however you refer to the field, it’s become a hugely significant part of investigative journalism in recent years. From finding initial leads, to building evidence relevant to an existing hypothesis, to verifying a piece of evidence found on social media – these skills can be used in many different ways for investigative reporting.

At the Centre for Investigative Journalism, we’ve been delivering training on these techniques for more than a decade to journalists and other researchers investigating in the public interest. What this experience has taught us, in turn, is that the core OSINT mindset is the most important learning goal.

While there is, of course, great value in learning tools and techniques that allow you to conduct online investigative research more effectively and efficiently right now, the field is especially dynamic. Good tools that work today may be behind financially inaccessible paywalls tomorrow, web infrastructure is subject to frequent change that means certain techniques become less reliable, new platforms spring up often with the potential to make whole sections of practice obsolete.

title: Building an Engaged Community through Collaboration and In-Depth Investigations, All While Maintaining a Sense of Humor
content:
“The thing we feared the most in the very beginning, given our relaxed vibe, was becoming too serious and turning into a bureaucratic office,” says Miglė Krancevičiūtė, co-founder of the Lithuanian investigative outlet Siena.

As we speak, she is leaning against a custom-printed pillow with a tongue-in-cheek quote — “financial cushion!” — from one of their recent investigations. Fans of their work, and follow-the-money anti-corruption investigations in general, can buy the cushion in their online shop for €25 (about $28).

Image: Screenshot from Siena’s online store

Founded in 2019, the nonprofit newsroom has taken part in hard-hitting investigations led by international networks, including projects like Dubai Unlocked, the FinCEN files, and the Pandora Papers, and in 2022, the outlet became one of GIJN’s members. But its core mission is to bring that networked journalism experience home to Lithuania.

To the west of the country, across the Baltic Sea, lies Sweden, where the team at Siena draws journalistic inspiration. On the other side of a forested border is Belarus, whose internationally sanctioned dictator is a target of numerous Siena investigations.
